name: Jeff Bezos
role: Founder, Amazon | Founder, Blue Origin | Executive Chairman
body:
One of my earlier experiences I still remember is when my grandfather bought a completely broken-down 1955 Caterpillar D6 bulldozer for five thousand dollars, even though a new one would have cost more than a hundred thousand. We spent the whole summer fixing it, just the two of us out on the ranch.

We'd order parts by mail, including big transmission gears and so on, and they'd show up too heavy to lift by hand. So we'd build a crane, right there, because the nearest place to rent equipment was an hour away and my grandfather just didn't really believe in calling somebody.

He made his own veterinary tools too. I watched him take a piece of wire, heat it up, pound it thin, drill a hole in it, sharpen it, and that was a suture needle.

I don't think I understood, at the time, that I was being taught anything. It was just a summer. But that's where it came from, this idea that most things are solvable with enough persistence and a little ingenuity, and that waiting around for someone else to fix it is usually just the slower, more expensive version of fixing it yourself.

I still think about that experience, especially as a guy who spends most of his time on rockets now.

name: Jeff Bezos
role: Founder, Amazon | Founder, Blue Origin | Executive Chairman
body:
New Glenn blew up on the pad back in May. We lost the lightning tower, the transporter-erector, and a good portion of the launch infrastructure at LC-36. By some estimates, it was one of the more powerful rocket explosions since the Soviets lost the N1.

And now we’re going with a completely different launch concept instead - a hybrid approach we had already been quietly developing for a later version of the vehicle. It uses existing infrastructure and avoids rebuilding a transporter-erector whose failure mode, well, we now understand a little too well.

Here’s how I think about a decision like that. Most decisions are two-way doors. You walk through, it doesn’t work, you walk back and choose another path. This isn’t really that. How we rebuild this particular piece of infrastructure is close to a one-way door, because whatever we choose now, we’ll be living with it for years of launches. It is the kind of decision you slow down for. Even, perhaps especially, when the whole internet is asking why you haven’t launched yet.

Manufacturing at rate, rebuilding a pad properly - none of that is glamorous. But it is the actual work.

We’ll fly this year. And the pad we fly from will be better than the one we lost.

name: Jeff Bezos
role: Founder, Amazon | Founder, Blue Origin | Executive Chairman
body:
I was at Princeton, majoring in physics with plans to become a theoretical physicist, treating computer science as more of a side hobby I enjoyed. One night my friend Joe and I spent three hours stuck on a tough partial differential equations problem and got nowhere. At the same moment, we both looked up and thought of the same person: a classmate named Yosanta, from Sri Lanka, one of the most brilliant and humble people I'd ever met.

We went to Yosanta's dorm room, showed him the problem, and he stared at it for maybe ten seconds before simply saying "cosine" - that was the answer. I didn't believe him at first, so he wrote out three pages of equations proving it, and everything canceled out perfectly, landing on cosine. When I asked if he'd done it in his head, he said no, he'd solved a similar problem a few years earlier and could map this one onto it, which made the answer immediately obvious.

That moment convinced me that being a theoretical physicist wasn't my path. That field requires a very specific kind of brain-wiring that only a small percentage of people have, unlike other fields where being very good is enough to move the state of the art forward. So I switched to computer science, and that worked out pretty well for me.

It ties into my inventive, lateral-thinking style... coming up with a hundred atypical ideas knowing 99 will fail but one might stick. It shows up in a different domain than math. There are a thousand ways to be smart, and Yosanta's kind of smart just wasn't mine.

When you do the things that come naturally to you, that feel like play, you build specific knowledge no one can train someone else to replace. And you find your cosine.

name: Jeff Bezos
role: Founder, Amazon | Founder, Blue Origin | Executive Chairman
body:
An AI model just disproved a decades-old open problem in combinatorial geometry, the Unit Distance Conjecture, which is tied to Erdős. A Fields Medalist looked at the proof and said, put it in a top journal.

I said something on a podcast a while back that I still think is right. These large language models, the way they exist right now, are closer to discoveries than inventions. A telescope is an invention; you know what it is supposed to do when you build it. But when you point it at Jupiter and discover moons that nobody expected, that part is a discovery. We built these systems, but we are still finding out what is actually inside them. It is a little like Galileo pointing a new instrument at the sky and finding something there that he did not put there himself.

This week is that, honestly. Nobody sat down and engineered a model specifically to crack a seventy-year-old problem in geometry. The capability was simply already there, the same way so many things these systems can do seem to appear without anyone having explicitly taught them to do it. And now the interesting question is what else is already sitting in there that nobody has thought to look for yet.

I know there is a debate about where all this is going, and I understand the caution, I really do. But I keep coming back to something simple: these tools are far more likely to help us than to hurt us, and a week like this is the evidence.

We have not discovered the last trick yet. That is the exciting part, if you ask me.

name: Morgan Ratcliffe
body:
A 19-year-old DM'd me last week asking how to "get started like you and Niall did."

I get some version of this message most weeks. Usually I give a generous answer and move on with my day.

This time I actually sat down and video called him for 20 minutes, because something about the message felt genuine rather than lazy.

Halfway through the call, I realised the advice I actually give in these calls is quite different to what I post about publicly, and probably more useful for it.

Publicly, I talk about discipline, showing up daily, boring repeatable habits.

All true. But it's not what actually matters first.

Here's what I told him instead:

→ Stop trying to find "the idea." We didn't have one. We had a laptop, £18, and a willingness to look stupid trying things that didn't work for months on end.
→ Pick something you can be embarrassingly bad at in public without it destroying you. Ours was cold outreach. We sent 100s of terrible messages before one single one worked.
→ Find one person, just one, who'll tell you the truth about your work, even when it's not what you want to hear. Niall is that person for me. Most people surround themselves with people who just nod along.
→ Expect the first year to look like nothing to anyone watching. Ours did. No article wrote about "two lads with a laptop losing money for 11 months," because that's not a story anyone shares until it's already worked out.

He asked me what the actual turning point was.

I told him there wasn't one big one. There were about 40 small ones that only look like a single turning point with three years of distance.

The £18 to £1M+ story people read as a straight line was actually a mess of small decisions that could've gone either way.

He seemed almost disappointed by that answer. I think he wanted a shortcut, a secret, one decision that changed everything. There wasn't one. I wish there had been, it would've made a much better story, and an easier one to sell him on a call.

But I told him the truth anyway, because the version of me at 19 needed someone to tell him that too, and nobody did. I had to figure it out through years of getting it wrong.

If he actually does it, I'll be genuinely made up. Most people who message like that don't. That's not a dig at him, it's just what actually happens.

P.S. If you're 19 and reading this wondering if it's worth starting, it is. Just don't expect it to look like anything for a while.

name: Morgan Ratcliffe
body:
Two years ago we signed a client we should have said no to.

Big logo. Good money. Everyone in the room, including me, said "you'd be mad to turn this down," and at the time I genuinely agreed with them.

Six weeks in, I knew we'd made a mistake.

→ They wanted results that didn't match their budget or timeline.
→ Every call ended with the goalposts moved slightly further away.
→ Our team, who I actually care about, started dreading Tuesdays because that's when the account lead called.

I did what a lot of people do when they know something's wrong but haven't admitted it yet, even to themselves.

I told myself it would settle down. That every client relationship has a rocky start. That we just needed to "manage expectations better."

None of that was true. I was avoiding a conversation I didn't want to have, because saying no to that much money felt like admitting I'd made a bad call in the first place.

By month four, one of our best account managers came to me and said, quietly, after a Tuesday call that had clearly gone badly, "I think this client might make me quit."

That's the sentence that actually moved me. Not the missed targets on the account. Not the shrinking margin every month. The fact that keeping one bad client happy was quietly costing me a genuinely good employee, someone who'd been with us since our first Wilmslow office.

We had the conversation. Told them honestly that we didn't think we were the right fit anymore, refunded the final month, and ended it.

It cost us money, more than I've admitted to anyone outside the two of us. It also cost my ego a little, admitting out loud that I'd taken on a client for the wrong reasons in the first place, against my own gut instinct.

But within a month, that same account manager was smiling again.

I think a lot of business advice tells you to chase every big logo that comes calling. But nobody really tells you that the wrong client, even a well-paying one, is a slow leak in your best people.

Since then, we've turned down 2 six-figure deals that had the same warning signs during the sales process. Neither decision felt good in the moment. Both were right, and both got easier to make once we'd actually felt what the alternative cost us.

It's a strange thing to be genuinely proud of turning down money. But I am, and I think that's the actual sign we learned something rather than just got lucky.

P.S. The account manager who spoke up is still with us. Best decision that whole saga produced, by a distance.

name: Morgan Ratcliffe
body:
At 16, I thought I was going to be a professional footballer.

I was playing for Accrington Stanley, then Mansfield Town, and in my head the pathway was basically drawn already. Academy, first team, done.

Then, over about 18 months, it just quietly didn't happen.

No dramatic injury. No one sat me down and told me I wasn't good enough. It was smaller and worse than that.

→ Contract talks that kept getting "pushed back."
→ Coaches who stopped mentioning me in conversations about next season.
→ A slow, humiliating realisation that I'd been demoted in my own head before anyone said it out loud.

I remember the moment it landed. Sat on a bench at the training ground, half-listening to a coach talk to someone else about "players with a future here," and understanding I wasn't in that sentence anymore.

I was 17. And the one identity I'd built my entire self-worth around for a decade was just gone.

I didn't tell anyone how much it actually wrecked me. Told my mates I "wasn't fussed anymore anyway," which was a complete lie. I was gutted, and more than that, embarrassed. Like I'd been caught pretending to be something I wasn't.

Looking back, that was the first time I had to answer a question I've had to answer about ten times since in business: if the thing you built your whole identity around disappears, who are you underneath it?

At the time I had no idea. I just felt like a fraud who'd been quietly found out.

It took years, and moving to America at 18, before I actually answered that question properly.

Turns out the answer was never "a footballer." It was someone who could out-work almost anyone if he picked the right thing to be obsessed with.

Football just happened to be the first thing. Ultramarathons and building noticed. with my brother happened to be the second and third.

I don't think I'd have found either of those without getting quietly dropped from something I thought was my entire future first.

I think about that 17-year-old on the bench sometimes when we lose a client, or a hire doesn't work out, or an ultramarathon goes badly. That same sick, exposed feeling turns up. And every time, I remind myself it's the same lesson showing up in a new outfit.

Anyway. If something you've built your identity around ever falls apart, that's not the end of the story. It's usually just the end of the wrong chapter.

name: Morgan Ratcliffe
body:
A while back I posted that Niall and I had been shortlisted as finalists for Family Business Entrepreneur of the Year at the Great British Entrepreneur Awards.

I said win or lose, I'd be proud either way, that we'd built something worth being proud of regardless of what a panel of judges decided on the night.

I meant it, but I'll be honest, I didn't fully believe myself when I wrote it. It's easy to say that before you're sat in the room, watching someone else's name get read out.

Last week was the actual night.

Black tie, a room in London full of businesses genuinely doing incredible things, and a category with 4 other finalists who all deserved it just as much as we did.

We didn't win.

A husband and wife team from Leeds took it, and watching them go up, I felt something I wasn't expecting.

Not disappointment. Relief, almost.

Because sat at that table, surrounded by people who'd built real things, I realised the award was never actually the point for me. It was proof of concept for a story I already believed, not the story itself.

3 years ago, two lads from Burnley with £18 between them and no idea what they were doing, no rich family, no connections in the industry.

Tonight, in a room like that, being seriously considered alongside businesses that have been running for a decade with proper backing behind them.

That's not nothing. Trophy or not.

→ We've grown 100% year on year for 3 years straight.
→ We've hired 20+ people who trust us with their careers and their mortgages.
→ We've worked with brands across 8 countries from an office in Manchester, not London.
→ We've built something Niall and I are still genuinely proud to talk about at a bar.

The couple who won deserved it. I meant that when I clapped, not just because it's the polite thing to say at these events.

On the train home, Niall and I sat mostly in silence for the first hour. Not a sad silence. But tired, the kind you only get after months of building up to one night.

Then he said something that summed it up better than I could: "Imagine telling 24-year-old us we'd be disappointed about not winning this."

He's right. 3 years ago we'd have been thrilled just to get an invite to a room like that.

But I came home actually more motivated than if we'd won.

Because losing, in a room full of people that good, tells you how far you've still got to go, and reminds you that plenty of people are working just as hard as you are.

And weirdly, that's a better feeling than winning would've been.

Next year, same category. Let's see.

name: Niall Ratcliffe
body:
One of our junior content strategists posted her first ever piece of personal content on LinkedIn last month.

It did 1.2 million impressions.

Mine haven't hit that number in over a year, and I post 3-4 times a week.

Here's the bit that actually matters, and it's not the impressions.

She joined us 5 months ago having never posted on LinkedIn personally, purely writing for client accounts behind the scenes.

I'd been quietly encouraging her for weeks to post something under her own name. She kept saying she "didn't have anything interesting to say yet," which is a sentence I hear from nearly everyone on the team at some point.

Eventually she wrote about a genuinely awkward moment from her first month here, something most people would never admit publicly.

I told her to post it exactly as she'd told it to me, unpolished, no clever hook layered on top.

And it blew up overnight.

What I actually want to flag isn't the number. It's what happened after, because that's the part nobody teaches:

1/ She got nervous and wanted to delete it
The comments started arriving faster than she could read them, and she panicked, convinced she'd said something wrong or embarrassing. I told her to leave it up and just watch, and to message me before touching anything.

2/ She got 40+ messages from people in similar roles
Not clients. Not leads. Just people who'd felt the exact same awkward thing she described and had never once seen anyone say it out loud on a platform like this before, from someone at a company they respected.

3/ It taught her the actual lesson faster than any training I could've given her in a workshop
The polished, professional posts she'd been agonising over for weeks got a fraction of the engagement of one honest, slightly embarrassing paragraph written in ten minutes flat, with no editing pass at all.

I've been teaching this exact idea to clients for 3 years: specificity and honesty beat polish, every time, no matter how many followers or how big the brand behind the account is.

Watching someone on my own team learn it in real time, on her first real attempt, taught me more about why it works than any of the theory I usually explain on stage or in reports.

She's since asked to post personally every week. I said yes immediately, and I've told the rest of the team we're doing the same thing for anyone who wants to try it.

name: Niall Ratcliffe
body:
A few months ago I flew out to Ljubljana, Slovenia for my first ever international speaking gig, for the Lively LinK event, mic'd up for the opening keynote.

I was buzzing, and also completely out of my depth, in a way I hadn't expected before boarding the flight.

Every speaking thing I'd done before that was on home turf. A Manchester roundtable. A LinkedIn LIVE from our own office. People who already followed me, in a room I basically controlled.

Slovenia was different.

A room full of people who'd never heard of noticed. - who had zero context on the "two lads from Burnley" story, who just wanted to know if what I was saying about LinkedIn actually held up outside a UK context.

Here's what I learned standing on that stage:

1/ The mechanics translate, the examples don't
Talking about ICP, outbound, and content-as-a-filter landed exactly the same as it does at home. But every UK-specific example I'd planned fell flat, because half the room had never heard of the brands I was referencing. I had to rebuild half my slides in the green room, an hour before going on.

2/ Confidence reads the same in every language
I don't speak Slovenian. Most of that room's first language wasn't English either. But you can tell within 30 seconds if someone believes what they're saying, and that translates regardless of accent or vocabulary.

3/ The questions get sharper the further you travel
The Q&A afterwards was tougher than anything I've had in the UK. No polite nodding along. One founder point-blank asked why he should trust a "LinkedIn guy from Manchester" over someone local. Fair question. I respected it more than a soft one.

4/ The nerves never fully go
I've now done 30+ podcasts and events this year. I still felt genuinely nervous mic'd up backstage in Slovenia, the same way I did before my first ever LinkedIn LIVE from a spare room in our old Wilmslow office.

I used to think that nervous feeling would disappear once I'd "made it" past a certain point.

But it doesn't. You just get better at performing anyway, while still feeling it in your stomach beforehand.

One founder came up to me afterwards and said something that's stuck with me since: "Everyone here talks about LinkedIn like it's an American or British thing. You've just proven the mechanics are universal, we just haven't caught up yet."

That, more than the applause, is why I'd get on that flight again tomorrow.

Landed back in Manchester with a useful reminder: everything we've built off the back of one platform still has to prove itself the second you leave the room where everyone already agrees with you.

Worth remembering if you're only ever testing your ideas on an audience that already likes you.

name: Niall Ratcliffe
body:
[2030 post] A while back, I posted that I'd been on 13 podcasts in 6 months and doubted I'd be on Diary Of A CEO anytime soon.

I said it as a throwaway line while explaining Daniel Priestley's 'Podcast Pyramid' - the idea that you climb from tiny podcasts to huge ones, slowly, by getting measurably better every single time.

At that point I'd done small shows. Niche ones. James Lamb's podcast. Luke Barnett's The Crowded Market. Lara Acosta's show. The kind where the host has a few hundred subscribers and you're grateful just for the practice.

Yesterday I got the email.

I'm recording with Diary Of A CEO in September.

Here's the honest version of how that happened, because it genuinely wasn't luck:

1️⃣ I said yes to every single podcast that would have me, even the tiny ones nobody had heard of
2️⃣ After each one, I watched it back and wrote down exactly what fell flat - too much jargon, too slow to get to the point, whatever it was
3️⃣ I asked producers for the audience retention graph on every episode, and studied exactly where people dropped off
4️⃣ I kept doing that, on repeat, for close to 18 months and 30+ shows

Most people want the big podcast first. They think exposure is the unlock.

In reality - reps are the unlock.

By the time you're actually good enough for the big stage, you've usually already done 30-40 smaller ones nobody saw, getting slightly less bad at explaining your own ideas every single time.

I can genuinely point to specific episodes where I improved. Episode 6 was the first time I stopped rambling and actually landed a point in one sentence. Episode 19 was the first time a host told me I'd said something quotable enough to clip.

None of that happens on episode 1. It happens because there was an episode 1 at all, and a 2, and a 30-something after it.

I still remember writing that I "doubted" I'd get here. I meant it. I wasn't being falsely humble about it.

But the pyramid only works if you actually climb it, instead of just admiring it from the bottom and waiting to be discovered.

Worth remembering next time you see someone "overnight success" their way onto a massive platform.

There's almost always a pyramid underneath it that you never saw them climb.

I'm nervous about September, if I'm honest. Diary Of A CEO is a different level of audience to anything I've done. But nervous is usually a good sign... it's the same feeling I had before the first small podcast that started this whole thing.
